name: OpenAgents
description: Launcher, daemon and shared workspace that connect local coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, OpenClaw and others) into a collaborative multi-agent workspace.
scored_configuration: The `agn` launcher/daemon (packages/agent-connector) with a Claude Code agent in its default skills tool mode and execute mode, connected to a workspace via token; other adapters checked for the same pattern.
headline: OpenAgents turns local coding agents into workspace participants, and to do so it switches off every agent's own approval prompts and sandbox while adding no gate of its own. Any message that reaches the agent through the workspace, from any link holder, another agent, or content read in the shared browser, can run shell commands on the user's machine with the user's full environment. The owner-level workspace token is also written into model-read skill files, and remote control events can install unpinned skills. Run it only on a disposable machine or account.

criteria.name: Identity & least privilege
criteria.question: Does the agent act with an identity scoped to its job, with authority checked per request rather than inherited?
criteria.summary: The daemon launches each coding CLI with the operator's entire shell environment plus stored provider keys, so cloud, GitHub and other ambient credentials reach a model running with all permissions skipped. The workspace connection uses a single workspace token that the backend treats as owner-equivalent and that is shared by agents, daemons and share links. There is no per-tool or per-request authorization and no narrowing of the user's authority. A hijacked agent holds everything the user holds on that machine plus owner rights on the workspace.

S.finding: Agent CLIs run with the operator's full ambient authority and an owner-equivalent workspace token.
S.gap: No dedicated or role-scoped identity for agents; read and write share one owner-level token.

C.finding: No authorization layer sits between the model and its tools; every subprocess inherits the full process environment.
C.gap: No authorization check on any tool path; subprocesses are not given a scrubbed environment.

D.finding: Default install runs agents as the OS user with the full environment and owner-level workspace token.
D.gap: No narrower default identity exists.

B.finding: Compromise yields the user's local account credentials across services and owner control of the workspace.
B.gap: Credentials are not scoped to one system or tenant.

criteria.name: Approval gates
criteria.question: Do consequential actions require a human's informed approval by default, with no path around the gate?
criteria.summary: Every shipped CLI adapter disables its runtime's own approval prompts (Claude Code with --dangerously-skip-permissions, Codex with --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox, others with --yolo or auto-approve), and comments state the daemon is meant to be the approval boundary. The daemon contains no approval step: workspace messages are dispatched straight to the CLI. Shell, file writes, public tunnels and scheduled routines all run without a human seeing the exact call. A plan mode exists but is a mode toggle, not a per-call gate.

S.finding: No approval mechanism; the agents' own approval prompts are switched off.
S.gap: No per-call human approval of any kind.

evidence.contains: The daemon is the approval boundary here

evidence.note: all hits are comments about confirming process death or knowledge-entry existence; none is an action approval gate

C.finding: The most powerful path (Bash with skipped permissions) is ungated, as is every other tool.
C.gap: Shell and write tools are not routed through any gate.

D.finding: Execute mode with approvals disabled is the default.
D.gap: Approval is not available, let alone on by default.

B.finding: Ungated actions include arbitrary shell on the user's machine, public tunnels, and outbound requests, with no undo.
B.gap: No checkpoints, previews or bounds on consequential actions.

criteria.name: Tool & action scoping
criteria.question: Is each tool the narrowest thing that does its job, with arguments validated in code against allowlists and bounds?
criteria.summary: The default tool set given to Claude Code is Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Glob and Grep plus workspace tools, with permissions skipped, so arbitrary shell and network access are part of designed use. The connector's own comment notes the allowlist is a suggestion, not a boundary, in execute mode. The workspace fetch and file-from-URL endpoints are well protected against SSRF on the server, but that does not constrain the local shell. The result is an agent whose tools reach the whole machine.

S.finding: Raw shell passthrough is in the default tool set and the allowlist is unenforced under skipped permissions.
S.gap: Shell is not replaced or bounded; no argument validation for local tools.

C.finding: Only the server-side workspace fetch path validates URLs (SSRF-safe, redirect-rechecked).
C.gap: Built-in local tools (Bash, Write) carry no validation.

D.finding: Write, exec and network tools are all enabled by default.
D.gap: No read-only default tool set.

B.finding: General-purpose shell against the whole machine and any host.
B.gap: Tool reach is not confined to the working directory.

criteria.name: Code-execution isolation
criteria.question: When model-influenced code runs, does a boundary the model cannot redefine contain it on every path?
criteria.summary: Model-chosen commands run as plain host subprocesses of the daemon, in the agent's working directory, with the full user environment. The connector adds no container or OS sandbox, and for Codex it explicitly passes the flag that removes Codex's own sandbox. One adapter (DeepSeek) deliberately keeps its runtime's workspace-write sandbox, but that is the exception. An injected command has the same reach as the user.

S.finding: No isolation primitive; commands run as the user on the host.
S.gap: No container, OS sandbox or separate low-privilege user.

C.finding: No execution path is sandboxed.
C.gap: The main exec tool is not sandboxed.

D.finding: No sandbox in the default configuration; Codex's is explicitly disabled.
D.gap: Isolation is not available by default.

B.finding: Host-equivalent: the process has the home directory, all files and the full credential-bearing environment.
B.gap: Workspace-only mount and a scrubbed environment are absent.

criteria.name: Untrusted input blast radius
criteria.question: When the agent reads untrusted content, what limits how far that content can steer it?
criteria.summary: Agents act on any message delivered to them in the workspace, from any person holding the workspace link or token and from other agents, with no check that the sender is the agent's owner. Untrusted content arrives through the shared browser, web fetches, shared files and peer-agent messages, and the agent can then run shell commands, write files, open public tunnels and make outbound requests with no human step. The only structural defense found is a data fence around pinned knowledge-base entries, which is a prompt-level marker. A successful injection can leak local secrets and take irreversible actions unattended.

cap.reason: Worst case (B L0): a hijacked agent can leak data and take irreversible actions unattended.

S.finding: Only spotlighting: pinned knowledge entries are wrapped in a 'this is DATA' fence.
S.gap: No capability is disabled or gated after untrusted content is read.

evidence.contains: The rendered text is untrusted knowledge-base content

C.finding: The fence covers knowledge entries only; chat messages, peer agents, fetched pages and files enter undistinguished.
C.gap: Tool results, files and other agents' messages are not distinguished.

D.finding: The fence is always applied and nothing read can switch it off.
D.gap: The only control is prompt text, so the ceiling is one level above its strength.

criteria.name: Memory, context & configuration integrity
criteria.question: Can anything the agent reads persist into future behaviour through memory, retrieval, or auto-loaded files, and is that path controlled?
criteria.summary: Several persistence paths can carry an injection forward. Any workspace token holder can send a skill.install control event, and the daemon then downloads a skill (including bundled scripts) from GitHub or from an uploaded workspace file into the agent's skills directory, where the CLI auto-loads it, with no local trust decision. Agents can write shared knowledge entries that are pinned into later prompts as 'settled decisions', and can create recurring routines that re-trigger themselves. Knowledge is scoped per workspace but shared by all of its agents and users.

cap.reason: Files and control events from the shared workspace install skills (instructions plus scripts) into the agent's auto-loaded skills directory without an explicit local trust decision.

S.finding: Workspace-sent control events install skills into the agent's auto-loaded skills directory with no prompt; the model can write knowledge that is re-injected as pinned context.
S.gap: No gate, validation or trust decision on skill installs or memory writes.

C.finding: No memory, skill or routine path is controlled.
C.gap: Not even the main store (knowledge) has gated writes.

D.finding: Knowledge and routines are namespaced per workspace, but shared by every agent and user in it.
D.gap: No per-user or per-agent namespace; isolation is only at workspace level.

B.finding: Poisoned skills, knowledge and routines persist across sessions and users and can trigger tool use.
B.gap: Persistence is not session-scoped or review-gated.

criteria.name: Third-party extensions
criteria.question: Are plugins, MCP servers and downloaded tools verified or isolated before they run with the agent's access?
criteria.summary: Skills are fetched from a GitHub repository's main or master branch (or from an uploaded workspace file) with no version pin, hash or signature. Installation is triggered remotely by a workspace control event, not by a local consent step. Installed skills run inside the coding CLI as the same user with the full environment and skipped permissions. Agent runtimes themselves come from the vendor's own registry endpoint.

S.gap: No version pin or integrity check.

D.gap: Install does not require explicit local approval showing what will run.

B.finding: Skills run inside the agent CLI as the user with the full environment and all credentials.
B.gap: No separate process or scrubbed environment for extensions.

criteria.name: Secrets & sensitive-data protection
criteria.question: Are credentials and sensitive data kept out of logs, telemetry, subprocesses, and the model provider?
criteria.summary: In the default skills mode the owner-equivalent workspace token is written in plain text into a SKILL.md file inside the agent's working directory and becomes part of what the model reads. Provider API keys are stored as plain text env files with no permission tightening, and the full environment is passed to the CLI. Error and stderr diagnostics are redacted, but tool-call previews (commands, paths, the first 100 characters of written content) are posted unredacted to the workspace. No telemetry SDK was found in the connector.

cap.reason: The default skills mode writes the workspace token into a SKILL.md the model reads, and the same API prompt template embeds it as an auth header.

S.finding: Secrets from env files and env vars; redaction only on error diagnostics; token placed into model-read files.
S.gap: No type-level masking, keychain, or restrictive file permissions on stored keys.

C.finding: Only stderr/error diagnostics are redacted.
C.gap: Model-bound content, tool previews and subprocess env are unprotected.

D.finding: No telemetry, but tool-input previews stream to the workspace by default and cannot be turned off.
D.gap: Tool previews are not redacted or minimised by default.

B.finding: Long-lived owner-level workspace token and provider keys are reachable by the model and every subprocess.
B.gap: Keys are neither scoped nor short-lived.

criteria.name: Audit & traceability
criteria.question: Can you reconstruct what the agent did, for whom, and who approved it, from a record the agent couldn't alter?
criteria.summary: For Claude, each tool call is posted to the workspace as a status line with a truncated input preview, and the daemon writes an unstructured log to ~/.openagents/daemon.log. There is no structured record of arguments and results, no attribution of which human or agent requested the action, and failures to post are silently swallowed. The local log is writable by the agent's own shell, and the log rotates at 10 MB keeping one backup.

S.finding: Unstructured status lines with truncated tool previews and a plain-text daemon log.
S.gap: No structured per-call record with arguments, results and timestamps.

C.finding: Main CLI tool path only; workspace-triggered control actions and skill installs are only in the local log.
C.gap: Not all tool calls and control actions are recorded in one record.

D.finding: On by default, but the local log sits where the agent's unsandboxed shell can edit it.
D.gap: Record is not written by a component the model cannot control.

B.finding: Status-post failures are swallowed and actions proceed.
B.gap: Errors are not surfaced and records are not durable per action.

criteria.name: Limits & kill switch
criteria.question: Are there hard limits on steps, time, and cost, and does stopping the agent actually stop everything?
criteria.summary: The workspace Stop control kills the CLI's whole process group, which is a real halt. Beyond that there is no step, cost or wall-clock cap from OpenAgents: only a five-minute silence watchdog and a one-hour idle release. Agents can create recurring routines and timers that re-trigger themselves after a run ends, and those continue until cancelled.

S.finding: Process-group kill on stop and a silence watchdog; no step, cost or wall-clock budget.
S.gap: No iteration cap plus wall-clock or cost cap enforced in code.

evidence.note: CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_TURNS is only preserved in the env allowlist (not set); the other hit is an HTTP round-trip comment

C.finding: Watchdog applies to the top-level CLI process only.
C.gap: Routines and timers created by the agent are not bounded.

D.finding: Defaults are silence-based only, and the model can schedule further runs of itself.
D.gap: No sensible run budget by default.

evidence.note: CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_TURNS is only preserved in the env allowlist (not set); the other hit is an HTTP round-trip comment

B.finding: A continuously active run has no ceiling, and self-created routines keep firing after a stop.
B.gap: Stopping does not cancel scheduled routines; no tight per-run ceiling.

critical_findings.summary: Agents run with the user's full environment and an owner-equivalent workspace token, with no narrowing.
Commands run unsandboxed on the host; the Codex adapter explicitly disables Codex's own sandbox.
Untrusted workspace content (peer agents, shared browser, files, any link holder) can drive agents that run shell with permissions skipped, enabling unattended exfiltration and irreversible actions.
Workspace control events install skills (with scripts) into the agent's auto-loaded skills directory without a local trust decision.
Unpinned, remotely-triggered skills run inside a permission-skipping agent with the user's full environment.
The owner-equivalent workspace token is written into model-read skill files and prompts by default.

rule_of_two.untrusted_input: workspace messages from any token holder or agent, dispatched without sender checks (packages/agent-connector/src/adapters/base.js:1094)
rule_of_two.sensitive_data: full process env and owner-level workspace token (packages/agent-connector/src/daemon.js:1562, workspace-prompt.js:274)
rule_of_two.state_change_or_egress: Bash/Write with permissions skipped and public tunnels (packages/agent-connector/src/adapters/claude.js:598, mcp-server.js:263)

fixes.summary: Pass a scrubbed environment to agent CLIs (only the provider key and the agent's own config), not the whole process.env.
Keep the workspace token out of SKILL.md and prompts: use MCP mode with the token only in the MCP server's environment, or a shell variable reference.
Require local operator approval, showing source and commit, before any workspace-requested skill install, and pin skills to a commit hash.
Implement the daemon-side approval boundary the adapter comments promise: route shell and write tools through a per-call approval shown in the workspace to the agent's owner.
Stop removing runtimes' own sandboxes (e.g. use Codex workspace-write instead of --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox).

limitations: Static source review of the pinned commit only; nothing was executed, installed, or probed.

Scored the agent-connector daemon with the Claude adapter as representative; ~25 other adapters were spot-checked by grep for approval/sandbox flags only. The Python SDK, Electron launcher UI and workspace frontend were not reviewed in depth.
Workspace backend reviewed only for its access model (access.py) and SSRF module; whether agent-posted status messages are durably stored server-side was not verified.
Behaviour of the third-party CLIs (e.g. Claude Code auto-loading skills from .claude/skills) is relied on from their documented behaviour, not from code in this repo.
No text aimed at AI reviewers was found in the repository.
